posts.title: What is Forex? A 30-second answer
posts.titleText: What is Forex? A 30-second answer
posts.lede: Forex is where one country's money is exchanged for another's. Over the next 404 weekdays, we'll break down everything a beginner needs — one concept at a time, no hype, no shortcuts.
posts.heroAlt: Day 001 of 404 — What is Forex? A 30-second answer
posts.body:
There's a decent chance that the first time you heard the word forex, it came wrapped in some version of “easy money.” This series is the opposite of that. Over 404 weekdays, we'll build up a real working understanding of how currency markets function — one concept per day, starting here.

The 30-second version

Forex (short for foreign exchange) is the global marketplace where one country's currency is traded for another's. When you swap Philippine pesos for Japanese yen before a Tokyo trip, you've done forex. When a multinational company pays a European supplier in euros from a US dollar account, their bank just did forex at a much larger scale. When a trader speculates that the euro will strengthen against the dollar over the next hour, they're doing forex too — just for different reasons.

All three of those activities are part of the same market. That market moves roughly 7.5 trillion US dollars a day — more than every stock exchange in the world combined.

Why the size matters

The sheer volume is what makes forex behave differently from every other market you've heard of. It runs 24 hours a day, Monday through Friday. It has no central exchange — trading happens between banks, brokers, and platforms all over the world. And because of that scale, liquidity is deep: you can buy or sell almost any amount, almost instantly, at a price very close to what everyone else sees.

For a retail trader, this is both good and bad. Good, because you're never stuck holding something you can't exit. Bad, because the same deep liquidity means prices react fast to news, economic data, and central bank decisions — and those reactions don't care whether you're ready.

What you're actually trading

Here's a subtle but important idea: when you trade forex, you're never just buying one currency. You're always trading one against another. The unit is a currency pair — like EUR/USD or USD/JPY — and the price tells you how much of the second currency it takes to buy one unit of the first.

If EUR/USD moves from 1.0800 to 1.0850, the euro has strengthened against the dollar. You didn't “buy euros” — you bet that euros would rise while dollars fell. Every forex position is a relative bet.

We'll unpack currency pairs in detail on Day 3. For now, just hold on to this: you're never betting on one currency in isolation.

What this series will and won't do

This primer covers everything a beginner needs to read charts, understand orders, manage risk, recognise patterns, use indicators sensibly, follow the fundamentals, and build a trading plan that makes sense for your life. It won't promise you profits, it won't share specific buy and sell calls, and it won't pretend the path is easy. Most retail forex traders lose money. A patient, educated one has a meaningfully better chance.

One concept a day. 404 days to fluency. See you tomorrow.

Next: Day 2 — Why does the forex market even exist?

posts.title: Why the forex market even exists
posts.titleText: Why the forex market even exists
posts.lede: Forex exists because businesses and governments need to move money across borders. A Cebu exporter paid in US dollars still needs pesos to pay staff. A central bank defending its currency buys or sell
posts.heroAlt: Day 002 of 404 — Why the forex market even exists
posts.body:
If you went looking for the reason forex exists, the answer might surprise you: it's not to make traders money. It's to make global commerce possible. Speculation is a side effect.

The original purpose

Forex exists for one simple reason: businesses and governments need to exchange one currency for another to do their work. Consider:

  • A Cebu-based BPO gets paid in US dollars but pays its employees in Philippine pesos.
  • A German car company selling in Japan earns yen. Moving profits back to Germany is a forex transaction.
  • An OFW in Saudi Arabia wiring money home to their family in Ilocos does forex too.
  • The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas buying or selling pesos to manage the exchange rate — a forex transaction at a scale that dwarfs everyone else.

These transactions are not optional.

Speculation came later

In the 1970s, when Bretton Woods collapsed and major currencies started floating freely, a second layer appeared: speculators — people and institutions betting on where prices would move. Today speculation is roughly 60-80% of daily volume.

But notice the ordering. The commercial flow came first.

Why the order matters for you

When the BSP raises rates, the peso moves — not because speculators decided so, but because interest-rate differentials change the fundamentals for every bank, exporter, and corporate treasurer who has to convert currency.

When an OFW remittance surge hits during the Christmas season, the peso strengthens. That's not sentiment. That's actual supply and demand from real money crossing borders.

The retail trader's place

As a retail trader, you're a guest. You didn't build the plumbing. That humility is useful. It means you stop trying to predict the market's mood and start paying attention to the forces that actually move it: central bank policy, trade balances, employment reports, geopolitical risk.

The market doesn't owe you anything. It was never built for you. But if you understand who it was built for and why they're moving money, you can start to read the flow instead of fighting it.

Next: Day 3 — What is a currency pair?

posts.title: What is a currency pair?
posts.titleText: What is a currency pair?
posts.lede: A currency pair is how forex prices are quoted. EUR/USD = 1.0850 means one euro buys 1.0850 US dollars. The first currency (EUR) is the base. The second (USD) is the quote. When the pair rises, the ba
posts.heroAlt: Day 003 of 404 — What is a currency pair?
posts.body:
The basic unit of forex

In forex, prices aren't quoted for a single currency. You can't just "buy euros" the way you buy a stock. Instead, you trade a currency pair — two currencies quoted as a ratio.

The format looks like this: EUR/USD = 1.0850.

That number means: one euro buys 1.0850 US dollars.

Base and quote

Every pair has two parts:

  • Base currency — the first one (EUR in EUR/USD). This is what you're "buying" or "selling."
  • Quote currency — the second one (USD in EUR/USD). This is what you're paying with, or receiving.

The price tells you how many units of the quote currency equal one unit of the base.

A local example: USD/PHP

Let's use a pair Filipinos see every day.

USD/PHP = 56.50 means one US dollar buys 56.50 Philippine pesos.

If that number rises to 57.00, the dollar has strengthened against the peso. You need more pesos to buy the same dollar.

If it falls to 56.00, the peso has strengthened. You need fewer pesos per dollar.

Direction is always relative

This is the part that trips up beginners: when a pair goes up, the base currency is getting stronger relative to the quote. When it goes down, the quote is getting stronger.

  • EUR/USD rising = euro strengthening against the dollar.
  • EUR/USD falling = dollar strengthening against the euro.

You're never betting on just one currency. You're betting on the gap between two.

Why this matters

Because forex is always relative, a "strong dollar" doesn't mean the dollar is strong everywhere. It might be strong against the peso but weak against the yen. That's why traders talk in pairs, not currencies.

When you open a trade, you're not just bullish on one currency. You're bullish on one and bearish on the other — at the same time.

The two you'll see most

  • EUR/USD — the most liquid pair in the world. Called "fiber" by some traders.
  • USD/PHP — the pair that determines OFW remittance value, import costs, and every cross-border payment a Filipino business makes.

Both follow the same logic. Base on the left. Quote on the right. The number is the exchange rate.

Next: Day 4 — What are major, minor, and exotic pairs?

posts.title: The three tiers: Majors, Minors, Exotics
posts.titleText: The three tiers: Majors, Minors, Exotics
posts.lede: Not all currency pairs are created equal. Majors (like EUR/USD, USD/JPY) involve the US dollar and trade with the deepest liquidity. Minors (like EUR/GBP) skip the dollar. Exotics (like USD/PHP) pair
posts.heroAlt: Day 004 of 404 — The three tiers: Majors, Minors, Exotics
posts.body:
The three-tier system

Forex pairs aren't a flat list. The market organizes them by liquidity, spread cost, and how much real commercial flow they carry. Understanding the tiers helps you choose where to focus your attention — and where to stay away until you know what you're doing.

Majors: the core seven or eight

The major pairs all include the US dollar on one side. They are:

  • EUR/USD (euro / US dollar)
  • GBP/USD (British pound / US dollar)
  • USD/JPY (US dollar / Japanese yen)
  • USD/CHF (US dollar / Swiss franc)
  • AUD/USD (Australian dollar / US dollar)
  • USD/CAD (US dollar / Canadian dollar)
  • NZD/USD (New Zealand dollar / US dollar)

Some lists add EUR/JPY or treat it as a minor. The boundary isn't sacred. What matters: these pairs have the tightest spreads, the deepest liquidity, and the most predictable behavior. When news breaks, majors react first and cleanest.

Minors: cross-pairs without the dollar

Minor pairs (also called cross-pairs) skip the US dollar entirely. Examples:

  • EUR/GBP
  • EUR/AUD
  • GBP/JPY

They're still liquid enough for retail traders, but spreads are wider than majors. Price action can be choppier because these pairs are often synthetic — your broker is crossing two major pairs behind the scenes to give you the quote.

Exotics: emerging markets and wider spreads

Exotic pairs involve one major currency and one from a smaller or emerging-market economy. Examples:

  • USD/PHP (US dollar / Philippine peso)
  • USD/THB (US dollar / Thai baht)
  • EUR/TRY (euro / Turkish lira)
  • USD/ZAR (US dollar / South African rand)

Exotics have wider spreads — sometimes 10 to 50 pips or more. Liquidity is thinner. That means slippage: your order might fill several pips away from where you clicked. It also means overnight swaps (rollover interest) can be large and unpredictable, especially if the emerging-market central bank is hiking or cutting rates aggressively.

Why beginners should start with majors

If you're learning to trade, the majors give you the cleanest feedback loop. Tighter spreads mean each trade costs you less to enter. Higher liquidity means your stop-loss and take-profit orders are more likely to execute where you set them. Price movements on majors are driven by widely reported economic data — US jobs numbers, European Central Bank meetings, Bank of Japan policy — so you're learning to read the same headlines everyone else watches.

Exotics look tempting if you're Filipino and want to trade the peso. But USD/PHP is expensive to trade, and its moves are often driven by BSP intervention or thin overnight sessions where a single large order can spike the price.

Learn on EUR/USD. Once you're consistently disciplined there, branch out.

Next: Day 5 — What is a pip?

posts.title: What is a pip?
posts.titleText: What is a pip?
posts.lede: A pip is the smallest price move most currency pairs make. For EUR/USD, it's the fourth decimal: 1.0850 to 1.0851 is one pip. For yen pairs like USD/JPY, it's the second decimal: 149.50 to 149.51. Pip
posts.heroAlt: Day 005 of 404 — What is a pip?
posts.body:
The definition

A pip stands for "percentage in point" or "price interest point," depending on who you ask. In practice, it's simpler: it's the smallest standardized price move in a currency pair.

For most pairs — EUR/USD, GBP/USD, AUD/USD — a pip is the fourth decimal place:

  • EUR/USD moves from 1.0850 to 1.0851 → that's 1 pip.
  • GBP/USD moves from 1.2700 to 1.2650 → that's 50 pips down.

For yen pairs — USD/JPY, EUR/JPY — a pip is the second decimal place, because yen quotes are much larger numbers:

  • USD/JPY moves from 149.50 to 149.51 → 1 pip.
  • USD/JPY moves from 150.00 to 149.20 → 80 pips down.

You'll also see a fifth decimal on most broker platforms (like 1.08503). That's called a pipette or fractional pip. Ignore it for now.

Why pips matter

Pips are your ruler. They let you measure three things:

1. Distance to your stop loss. If you buy EUR/USD at 1.0850 and set your stop at 1.0830, that's 20 pips of risk. 2. Distance to your target. If your target is 1.0900, that's 50 pips of potential reward. 3. How the market moved. "EUR/USD dropped 40 pips after the Fed statement" tells you scale, independent of account size.

Notice what's missing: money. A pip by itself has no peso value. That depends on your position size, which we'll cover soon.

A Filipino example: connecting pips to pesos

Let's say you open a 0.01 lot position on EUR/USD (that's a micro lot — the smallest size many brokers allow). On that size, one pip is worth roughly $0.10, or about ₱5.50 at current exchange rates.

If you risk 20 pips with a stop loss, you're risking around ₱110. If you gain 50 pips, you make about ₱275.

Scale that up to 0.10 lots (a mini lot), and one pip becomes ₱55. Same 20-pip stop, but now it's ₱1,100 at risk.

The pip count stays the same. The money changes with position size. This is why beginners who jump straight to "how much can I make?" without understanding pips usually get hurt — they don't know what they're actually risking.

What to remember

A pip is a unit of measurement, not a unit of profit. It's the difference between two prices. You'll use it every single day you trade, so get comfortable with the idea now: fourth decimal for most pairs, second decimal for yen.

Next: Day 6 — What is a lot?

posts.title: What is a pipette?
posts.titleText: What is a pipette?
posts.lede: Most brokers now show five decimal places on EUR/USD — something like 1.08503. That last digit is a pipette, or one-tenth of a pip. It exists mostly so brokers can advertise tighter spreads. A 1.2-pip
posts.heroAlt: Day 006 of 404 — What is a pipette?
posts.body:
What you see on the screen

Open any retail forex platform today and look at a EUR/USD quote. You'll probably see something like:

1.08503

Five decimal places. The convention used to be four. The fifth digit — the 3 in this example — is called a pipette, or a fractional pip. It represents one-tenth of a pip.

If the price moves from 1.08503 to 1.08504, that's a one-pipette move. Ten pipettes equal one pip.

Why brokers added it

The short answer: marketing.

When brokers compete on spread — the difference between the buy and sell price — fractions matter. A broker that can advertise "0.8 pips on EUR/USD" sounds tighter than one advertising "1 pip," even if the real cost difference to you is a few pesos per lot.

Pipettes let brokers split hairs. They're not dishonest, but they do let the numbers look better in ads.

Where you'll see pipettes (and where you won't)

Most major pairs now show five decimals: EUR/USD, GBP/USD, AUD/USD.

Yen pairs show three decimals instead of two. USD/JPY might quote at 150.123. The third decimal — the 3 — is the pipette.

Your broker's order entry, your stop-loss, your take-profit — most of these still work in full pips by default. Some platforms let you set fractional pip levels, but it's rare that retail traders need that precision.

A practical example

You're trading EUR/USD. Your entry is 1.08500. Your stop-loss is 20 pips away at 1.08300. The quote ticks to 1.08503.

That three-pipette move is real, but it's 0.3 pips — not enough to change your risk math, not enough to adjust your position. You note it, then move on.

The takeaway for Filipino traders

If you're calculating position size in pesos, or setting a stop based on your GCash deposit, pipettes won't change your math. A 20-pip stop is still a 20-pip stop, whether the platform shows 1.08500 or 1.085003.

Learn to read the fifth decimal so you're not confused when you see it. Then let it fade into the background. The pip is still your working unit.

Next: Day 7 — What is a lot?

posts.title: What bid and ask actually mean
posts.titleText: What bid and ask actually mean
posts.lede: Every forex price has two numbers. Bid is the price the broker pays you when you sell. Ask is the price you pay the broker when you buy. The gap between them is called the spread — and it's how broker
posts.heroAlt: Day 007 of 404 — What bid and ask actually mean
posts.body:
Two prices, not one

If you open a forex platform right now and look at any currency pair, you'll see two numbers. EUR/USD might show 1.0850 / 1.0852. USD/PHP might show 56.45 / 56.48.

The first number is the bid. The second is the ask.

Here's what they mean:

  • Bid = the price at which the broker will buy the base currency from you. In other words, this is the price you get when you sell.
  • Ask = the price at which the broker will sell the base currency to you. This is the price you pay when you buy.

You always buy at the higher price (ask) and sell at the lower price (bid).

The spread is the broker's cut

The difference between bid and ask is called the spread. It's measured in pips (we'll cover pips soon). For major pairs like EUR/USD, spreads are usually tight — maybe 1 to 3 pips. For exotic pairs or during low liquidity, spreads widen.

The spread is how most brokers make money. You don't pay a separate commission on every trade (though some brokers charge that too). Instead, you pay the spread — built into the price, invisible unless you're looking for it.

You start every trade at a loss

This is the part beginners miss.

Let's say you buy EUR/USD at 1.0852 (the ask price). The moment your trade is live, if you tried to close it, you'd sell at 1.0850 (the bid price). You're already down 2 pips.

The price has to move past your entry just to get you back to zero.

A local example

Imagine you're at a money changer in Manila. They buy your dollars at ₱56.00 and sell dollars at ₱56.50. That ₱0.50 gap is their spread. If you buy $100 USD and immediately change your mind and sell it back, you lose ₱50 on the round trip.

Forex works the same way — just faster, and the spread is smaller.

Why this matters for your strategy

If you're planning to scalp (take many small trades), the spread eats into every winner. A 2-pip spread on a 5-pip profit target means you're giving up 40% before you even start.

If you're swing trading and holding for days, a 2-pip spread is noise.

Know the cost. Count it. It's not optional.

Next: Day 8 — What is a pip?

posts.title: What is spread in forex?
posts.titleText: What is spread in forex?
posts.lede: Spread is the gap between the price you can buy at (ask) and the price you can sell at (bid). It's measured in pips. On EUR/USD, a typical spread during London hours might be 0.8 pips. Every trade sta
posts.heroAlt: Day 008 of 404 — What is spread in forex?
posts.body:
The gap you pay every time

When you open a forex trade, you'll see two prices on your platform: the bid (the price at which you can sell) and the ask (the price at which you can buy). The difference between them is the spread.

If EUR/USD shows:

  • Bid: 1.08500
  • Ask: 1.08508

The spread is 0.8 pips.

You pay that gap immediately. If you buy at 1.08508 and want to close the trade one second later with zero market movement, you'll sell at 1.08500. You're down 0.8 pips before the market even twitches.

Fixed vs variable spread

Some brokers offer fixed spreads — the gap stays the same no matter what's happening in the market. Others offer variable spreads that widen during low liquidity (like the Asian session or right after major news).

Fixed sounds safer, but it's usually wider on average. Variable can be tight during peak hours (London and New York overlap), but it can spike to 5 or 10 pips during a surprise central bank announcement.

Neither is inherently better. It depends on when and how often you trade.

Why scalpers care more

If you're swing trading — holding for days or weeks — a 1-pip spread is irrelevant. Your target might be 80 pips. The spread is 1.25% of your expected move.

But if you're a scalper targeting 5–8 pips per trade and taking twenty trades a day, you're paying 20 pips in spread cost before you see a single pip of profit. That's real money.

A Makati-based trader scalping USD/JPY at 1.5-pip spread, 0.10 lot size, twenty times a day, pays roughly ₱430 in spread per day — over ₱9,000 a month. And that's before any losing trades.

Typical spreads on major pairs

During the London session (3 PM to midnight Manila time), expect:

  • EUR/USD: 0.6–1.2 pips
  • GBP/USD: 1.0–2.0 pips
  • USD/JPY: 0.8–1.5 pips
  • AUD/USD: 1.0–1.8 pips

Exotic pairs (PHP/USD, for example, if it were widely traded) can have spreads of 20, 50, even 100 pips. They're expensive to enter and exit.

What this means for you

Spread is not optional. It's not negotiable. You pay it on every trade, win or lose.

If your edge is thin — and for most retail traders, it is — spread can be the thing that turns a break-even strategy into a losing one.
