posts.title: Why forex is a 24-hour market
posts.titleText: Why forex is a 24-hour market
posts.lede: Forex trades 24 hours a day, Monday through Friday, with no central exchange. It opens in Sydney Sunday evening (UTC), rolls through Tokyo, London, and New York, then closes Friday afternoon in New Yo
posts.heroAlt: Day 009 of 404 — Why forex is a 24-hour market
posts.body:
No closing bell

Unlike the Philippine Stock Exchange, which opens at 9:30 AM and closes at 3:30 PM Manila time, the forex market has no central building and no official closing time during the trading week. It runs continuously from Monday morning in Sydney (which is late Sunday evening in most of the world) through Friday afternoon in New York.

This happens because forex is a decentralized, over-the-counter (OTC) market. Trades happen directly between banks, brokers, corporations, and retail platforms scattered across every timezone. As one financial center winds down, another is waking up.

The four major sessions

The 24-hour cycle is typically divided into four overlapping sessions, named after the major financial centers:

  • Sydney – Opens first, relatively low volume.
  • Tokyo – The Asian session; yen pairs and regional flow.
  • London – The heavyweight. Roughly 35% of daily forex volume happens here.
  • New York – Overlaps with London for several hours; highest combined liquidity.

Each session has its own character. London moves fast. Tokyo can be quieter. New York often sees sharp moves when US economic data drops at 8:30 AM Eastern.

What this means for Philippine-based traders

Manila is UTC+8, the same timezone as Singapore and Hong Kong. That puts you in a useful position:

  • Tokyo session runs during your morning and early afternoon.
  • London session opens around 3 PM Manila time.
  • New York session opens around 8 PM Manila time (or 9 PM during US daylight saving).

If you work a standard office job, you're home when London and New York overlap — the most liquid window of the day. Many Filipino retail traders do exactly this: they trade in the evening, after dinner, when EUR/USD and GBP/USD are moving.

Why 24 hours matters (and why it doesn't)

The fact that the market is always open does not mean you should always be watching it. In fact, the opposite is often smarter. Not all hours are equal. Volume, volatility, and the behavior of specific pairs change depending on which session is active.

Tomorrow we'll break down what each session looks like in detail, and which pairs tend to move when.

Next: Day 10 — The four forex sessions in detail

posts.title: The four trading sessions and why they matter
posts.titleText: The four trading sessions and why they matter
posts.lede: Forex runs 24 hours, but it's not equally active all day. The market moves through four sessions: Sydney, Tokyo, London, New York. The London–New York overlap (8:00 PM–12:00 midnight PHT) sees the hea
posts.heroAlt: Day 010 of 404 — The four trading sessions and why they matter
posts.body:
Why sessions matter

Forex is a 24-hour market, but it's not a flat hum of constant activity. Volume, volatility, and liquidity rise and fall as financial centers wake up and go to sleep. Understanding the rhythm helps you avoid trading when nothing is happening — or worse, when spreads widen because liquidity has dried up.

The market is commonly divided into four overlapping sessions, named after major financial hubs: Sydney, Tokyo, London, and New York.

The four sessions (in Philippine Time)

Here's when each session opens and closes, adjusted to PHT (UTC+8):

  • Sydney: 5:00 AM – 2:00 PM PHT
  • Tokyo: 7:00 AM – 4:00 PM PHT
  • London: 3:00 PM – 12:00 midnight PHT
  • New York: 8:00 PM – 5:00 AM PHT (next day)

Notice the overlaps. Tokyo and London overlap from 3:00 PM to 4:00 PM. London and New York overlap from 8:00 PM to midnight. That second overlap — London–New York — is the busiest window in the entire 24-hour cycle. Roughly 70% of all forex volume happens when both are open.

Which pairs move in which session

Not all currency pairs are equally active at all times. Here's the rough guide:

  • Tokyo session: USD/JPY, AUD/JPY, NZD/USD. Asian pairs and anything involving the yen.
  • London session: EUR/USD, GBP/USD, EUR/GBP. The euro and pound wake up here.
  • New York session: USD/CAD, and continued heavy flow in EUR/USD and GBP/USD.
  • Sydney session: AUD/USD, NZD/USD. Thin overall, but Oceania pairs can move on local data releases.

If you're trading EUR/USD at 9:00 AM Manila time, you're in the tail end of Sydney and early Tokyo — Europe is asleep. The pair might drift 10–15 pips all morning. But come 8:00 PM, when London and New York overlap, that same pair can move 50 pips in an hour.

Practical advice for Philippine-based traders

If you work a typical 9-to-5 and get home around 7:00 PM, you're actually in a good time zone for part-time trading. The London–New York overlap starts at 8:00 PM. That's prime time.

If you're awake during Tokyo hours (morning to mid-afternoon), focus on yen pairs or AUD/NZD crosses. Don't force a EUR/USD trade at 10:00 AM and wonder why nothing's happening.

If you're a night owl or graveyard-shift worker, you have access to New York's second half and the quiet handoff into Sydney. Liquidity thins out after midnight PHT, but economic news from the U.S. (non-farm payrolls, Fed statements) often drops between 8:30 PM and 10:00 PM Manila time — right in that overlap.

The quiet periods

The slowest time globally is the gap between New York's close and Tokyo's open — roughly 5:00 AM to 7:00 AM PHT. Spreads widen. Prices can be erratic on low volume. Unless you have a specific reason (like holding a swing trade through the rollover), there's little edge in trading that window.

Next: Day 11 — What is a pip?

posts.title: What is liquidity in forex?
posts.titleText: What is liquidity in forex?
posts.lede: Liquidity is how much you can trade without moving the price. High liquidity means tight spreads and instant fills. Low liquidity — during Asian lunch or before New York opens — means wider spreads, o
posts.heroAlt: Day 011 of 404 — What is liquidity in forex?
posts.body:
What liquidity means

Liquidity is the ability to buy or sell an asset without significantly moving its price. In forex, high liquidity means:

  • Tight bid-ask spreads (the gap between the price you can buy and the price you can sell).
  • Orders fill instantly at the price you expect.
  • Large positions can enter or exit without slippage.

Low liquidity is the reverse: spreads widen, fills are unpredictable, and even a modest trade can push the price against you.

Why liquidity changes by the hour

Forex runs 24 hours, but not all hours are equal. Liquidity depends on who is awake and trading.

High liquidity windows:

  • London session open (3:00 p.m. to midnight Manila time) — European banks, hedge funds, and corporates are active.
  • New York overlap with London (8:00 p.m. to midnight Manila time) — the busiest four hours of the day. EUR/USD, GBP/USD, and USD/JPY spreads are at their tightest.

Low liquidity windows:

  • Asian lunch (roughly 12:00 p.m. to 2:00 p.m. Manila time) — Tokyo traders step away. Spreads widen.
  • Pre-New York, post-Tokyo close (5:00 a.m. to 8:00 a.m. Manila time) — the market drifts. Price can whipsaw on thin volume.
  • Sunday evening (as the market opens) — liquidity is thin until Tokyo ramps up.

If you're day trading from Manila, this matters. A strategy that works beautifully at 9:00 p.m. (New York morning) may bleed money at 6:00 a.m.

Real-world example: GCash remittance and USD/PHP liquidity

Imagine you're a freelancer receiving USD payments and converting to pesos via your bank or an app. You'll notice the exchange rate is slightly worse than the "market rate" you see on Google. Part of that gap is the spread — and spreads are wider on USD/PHP than on major pairs like EUR/USD, because USD/PHP has lower liquidity.

Now imagine trading USD/PHP as a retail forex position at 3:00 a.m. Manila time. Liquidity is even thinner. Your 10,000-unit order might move the price by several pips. Your stop-loss, set at 56.75, gets filled at 56.78 because there weren't enough orders sitting at 56.75.

That's slippage. And slippage is a tax on low-liquidity trades.

When to avoid trading

You don't need to trade every hour the market is open. In fact, you shouldn't.

Avoid:

  • Major pairs during Asian lunch if you're scalping tight ranges.
  • Exotic or minor pairs outside their regional session (e.g., USD/ZAR at 2:00 a.m. Johannesburg time).
  • The first 10–15 minutes after major news releases, when liquidity vanishes and spreads spike.
  • Sunday evening opens, unless you have a specific reason.

Liquidity is invisible until it's not

Most beginners don't notice liquidity — until a stop-loss gets hit five pips away from where it was set, or a limit order never fills even though price "touched" the level on the chart.

That's low liquidity at work. The market didn't cheat you. You traded at the wrong time.

Next: Day 12 — What is a pip?

posts.title: What is a forex broker?
posts.titleText: What is a forex broker?
posts.lede: A forex broker is the company that executes your trade and holds your deposit. You can't call up Deutsche Bank and ask to trade EUR/USD with ₱5,000. The broker is your access point. Two rough models e
posts.heroAlt: Day 012 of 404 — What is a forex broker?
posts.body:
Why you need a broker

Retail traders can't access the interbank forex market directly. You're not going to call up HSBC or JPMorgan and ask to trade 0.01 lots of GBP/USD with ₱5,000. That's where a forex broker comes in: they aggregate liquidity, provide a trading platform, hold your deposit as margin, and execute your orders.

In short, the broker is your access point to the market.

Two rough models

Not all brokers operate the same way. The difference comes down to what happens after you click buy or sell.

### Dealing Desk (Market Maker)

In this model, the broker takes the opposite side of your trade. If you buy EUR/USD, the broker sells it to you — from their own book. They may hedge some of that risk by offsetting with other clients or taking positions in the interbank market, but they don't have to.

This creates an obvious conflict of interest: your loss is their gain. If you lose ₱10,000, the broker keeps it (minus any hedging costs). If you win ₱10,000, the broker pays you out of their pocket.

Not all dealing-desk brokers are predatory. Many are regulated and operate transparently. But the incentive structure is worth understanding.

### STP / ECN

Straight-Through Processing (STP) and Electronic Communication Network (ECN) brokers route your order to a pool of liquidity providers — banks, hedge funds, other brokers. You're trading against that pool, not against the broker.

The broker earns money from spreads (a small markup on the price) or a commission per trade. Whether you win or lose doesn't affect their revenue. They profit from your volume, not your losses.

This model tends to offer tighter spreads, faster execution, and less conflict of interest — but it often requires higher minimum deposits and charges explicit commissions.

A Filipino scenario

Imagine you're an OFW in Dubai. You open an account with a dealing-desk broker offering ₱500 minimum deposit and no commissions. It looks friendly. But when you start winning consistently, you notice slippage, requotes, or sudden spread widening during volatile hours.

Now imagine the same trader with an STP broker. Minimum deposit is ₱5,000, and you pay $3.50 per standard lot. But your orders fill fast, spreads stay tight, and the broker doesn't care whether you win — they already earned their commission.

Neither is automatically better. It depends on your capital, your strategy, and how much you trust the counterparty.

What to ask

Before you deposit:

  • Does the broker take the other side of my trade, or route it to liquidity providers?
  • How do they make money — spreads, commissions, or both?
  • Are they regulated by a credible authority (ASIC, FCA, CySEC)?
  • What happens to my deposit if the broker goes under?

Most retail traders pick a broker based on signup bonuses or flashy ads. That's backward. Start with the business model.

Next: Day 13 — What is leverage?

posts.title: ECN vs Market Maker: what's the difference?
posts.titleText: ECN vs Market Maker: what's the difference?
posts.lede: Not all brokers work the same way. An ECN broker routes your order to external banks and liquidity providers, charges you a commission, and doesn't care whether you win. A market maker takes the oppos
posts.heroAlt: Day 013 of 404 — ECN vs Market Maker: what's the difference?
posts.body:
Two ways brokers make money

When you open a forex trade, someone has to be on the other side. The question is: who?

The answer determines how your broker makes money — and whether their incentives align with yours.

There are two dominant models in retail forex: ECN/STP brokers and market makers. They look similar on the surface. They are not.

ECN and STP brokers

ECN stands for Electronic Communication Network. STP means Straight-Through Processing. In practice, both terms describe brokers that route your order to external liquidity providers — banks, hedge funds, other traders.

Here's what happens when you place a buy order on EUR/USD with an ECN broker:

1. Your order is sent to a pool of liquidity providers. 2. The best available price is matched. 3. You pay a commission — usually $3 to $7 per standard lot, round-turn. 4. The broker earns that commission whether you win or lose.

Notice the last point. The broker has no financial interest in the outcome of your trade. You are not their counterparty.

Market makers

A market maker broker takes the opposite side of your trade. When you buy, they sell to you. When you sell, they buy from you.

They don't charge commission. Instead, they widen the spread slightly and pocket the difference. More importantly: if you lose, they keep your money. If you win, they pay you out of their own pocket — unless they hedge your trade externally, which cuts into their margin.

This creates a structural conflict of interest.

Why it matters for scalpers

If you're trading once a week and holding for days, broker type might not make much difference. But if you're a scalper — entering and exiting multiple times a day, targeting 5–15 pips — execution quality is everything.

Market makers have been known to:

  • Requote prices during fast markets
  • Widen spreads when you're in profit
  • Reject or delay orders from consistently winning accounts

Not all market makers do this. But the incentive is baked into the model.

### A Filipino example

Imagine you're a consistent scalper in Makati. You make 15 trades a week, average 8 pips profit per trade. Over two months, your account is up 18%. Then your broker — a market maker — starts widening your EUR/USD spread from 1.2 pips to 2.8 pips, but only on your account. Your edge evaporates.

That's not paranoia. It's happened to enough traders that the pattern is well documented.

With an ECN broker, your success costs them nothing. You pay the same commission whether you win ₱500 or lose ₱5,000.

How to tell which model your broker uses

Check these signs:

  • Commission charged per trade? Likely ECN/STP.
  • "Zero commissions" but wider spreads? Likely market maker.
  • Variable spreads that widen during news? Could be either, but ECN brokers show raw spreads from the market.
  • Fixed spreads no matter what? Almost certainly market maker.

Most brokers will state their model in fine print, but marketing language can be vague. Look for phrases like "A-book" (ECN) vs "B-book" (market maker).

Which should you choose?

If you're learning and trading small size, a market maker might be fine — lower minimum deposits, simpler fee structure.

If you plan to scalp, trade frequently, or grow past beginner size, an ECN broker will save you money and frustration in the long run.

Your broker's job is to give you access to the market — not to bet against you.

Next: Day 14 — What is a pip?

posts.title: Why regulation matters more than you think
posts.titleText: Why regulation matters more than you think
posts.lede: A regulated broker — FCA in the UK, ASIC in Australia, BSP here in the Philippines — must hold capital reserves, keep your funds separate from theirs, and answer to a government authority. An unregula
posts.heroAlt: Day 014 of 404 — Why regulation matters more than you think
posts.body:
The unsexy truth

Regulation is boring. It doesn't show up in YouTube thumbnails. It won't improve your win rate. But it's the single most important filter you can apply when choosing where to put your money.

Here's why.

What regulation actually does

When a broker is regulated by a recognized authority — the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) in the UK, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC), the Cyprus Securities and Exchange Commission (CySEC), or the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) — they are required by law to:

  • Hold minimum capital reserves. They can't operate on fumes. If they go under, there's a buffer.
  • Segregate client funds. Your deposit sits in a separate account, not mixed with the broker's operating cash. If the company collapses, your money is ringfenced.
  • Submit to regular audits. Regulators check the books. Brokers can't cook the numbers indefinitely.
  • Offer dispute resolution. If something goes wrong — a withdrawal is blocked, a trade is misquoted — you have a formal channel to escalate.

None of this guarantees you'll make money. It guarantees the game isn't rigged from the start.

What happens without regulation

Offshore brokers — registered in jurisdictions with no real oversight — often advertise better conditions: tighter spreads, higher leverage, faster execution. Some are legitimate. Many are not.

The problem is simple: no regulator means no recourse.

If an unregulated broker decides not to process your withdrawal, you have no one to call. No ombudsman. No government body. You're done.

This has happened to Filipino traders more times than anyone wants to count. A broker offers 1:1000 leverage and a $10 minimum deposit. You fund the account via a payment processor you've never heard of. You make a few good trades. Then you try to withdraw, and the broker goes silent. Or the website goes down. Or they ask for "verification documents" that never get approved.

You just donated your money.

A local example

The BSP doesn't regulate many forex brokers directly yet, but they do regulate banks and remittance channels that brokers use to move peso deposits. If a broker operating in the Philippines is working through a BSP-supervised bank, that's a meaningful data point. It means they're not operating in total shadow.

Compare that to a broker with a Seychelles license and a Gmail support address.

The trade-off is real

Regulated brokers cost more to run. That cost gets passed to you in the form of slightly wider spreads or lower maximum leverage. If you're in the EU, for example, retail leverage is capped at 1:30 under ESMA rules.

That feels restrictive — until you remember that most traders who blow up do so because of high leverage, not in spite of it.

The bottom line

Your broker is the infrastructure. You can have the best strategy, the cleanest discipline, and a 70% win rate — but if your broker disappears, you have nothing.

Check the regulator. Google the license number. Make sure the website of the regulator lists that broker by name. It takes five minutes and might save you everything.

Next: Day 15 — What is a pip?

posts.title: What is swap and why does it matter?
posts.titleText: What is swap and why does it matter?
posts.lede: Hold a forex position past 5pm New York time and your broker applies a swap — a small credit or debit based on the interest-rate gap between the two currencies. Long the higher-yielding currency? You
posts.heroAlt: Day 015 of 404 — What is swap and why does it matter?
posts.body:
What swap is

When you hold a forex position past 5pm New York time (that's 6am Manila the next day), your broker applies a swap — also called rollover. It's a small credit or debit that shows up in your account balance, separate from the profit or loss of the trade itself.

Swap exists because every forex trade is technically two things at once: you borrow one currency to buy another. If you hold that position overnight, the market charges or pays you the interest-rate differential between the two.

How it works in practice

Let's say you go long on USD/PHP (you're buying dollars, selling pesos).

  • If the US Federal Reserve's interest rate is higher than the BSP's rate, you earn a small positive swap every night you hold the trade.
  • If the peso rate is higher, you pay.

The size of the swap depends on:

  • The interest-rate gap between the two currencies
  • Your position size
  • Your broker's markup (yes, they take a cut)

Why Wednesday is different

Forex markets are closed Saturday and Sunday, but interest accrues every calendar day. To account for that, brokers apply triple swap on Wednesday — one day's worth for Wednesday itself, plus Saturday and Sunday.

If you're holding a position with negative swap, that Wednesday hit is three times larger.

Who should care

Scalpers and day traders: Swap is invisible to you. You're in and out in minutes or hours. Ignore it.

Swing traders: If you hold positions for days or weeks, swap becomes part of your trade math. A position that earns ₱50 per day in swap over two weeks adds ₱700 to your result — or subtracts it, if the swap is negative.

Carry traders: Some traders build entire strategies around positive swap, going long high-yielding currencies against low-yielding ones and holding for months. It works — until the exchange rate moves against you faster than the swap can compensate.

A real example

Imagine you're long USD/PHP at 56.50, holding 1 standard lot (100,000 units). The interest-rate differential gives you a positive swap of roughly ₱80 per night (this is illustrative; real swap varies by broker and current rates).

Hold for 10 days = ₱800 in swap income. But if the pair drops 50 pips against you, you've lost ₱2,800 in price movement. Swap didn't save you.

The lesson: swap is real, but it's never the main event. Price movement is.

Where to find your broker's swap rates

Most brokers publish a swap table showing the credit or debit per lot per night for every pair. It's usually buried in the trading platform specs or the broker's website. Check it before you hold anything overnight.

Next: Day 16 — What is a pip, exactly?

posts.title: How brokers charge: commissions vs spreads
posts.titleText: How brokers charge: commissions vs spreads
posts.lede: Brokers make money two ways. Standard accounts widen the spread and charge no commission. ECN accounts give you raw spreads but charge a fixed fee per lot — often $3 to $7 round-turn. For scalpers, th
posts.heroAlt: Day 016 of 404 — How brokers charge: commissions vs spreads
posts.body:
Two ways brokers get paid

Every forex broker needs to make money. There are no free lunches. The question is how they charge you, and whether that structure matches the way you intend to trade.

There are two dominant models:

### 1. Standard (or market-maker) accounts

You see a spread — the difference between the buy price and the sell price. That spread is wider than the "raw" interbank spread. The broker keeps the difference. You pay no explicit commission. Your statement looks clean.

Example: EUR/USD might show a 1.5-pip spread. If the interbank spread is 0.2 pips, the broker's cut is roughly 1.3 pips per side.

### 2. ECN (or raw-spread) accounts

You see the tight interbank spread — sometimes as low as 0.0 to 0.3 pips on major pairs. But the broker charges a commission per lot traded, often $3 to $7 round-turn (open + close).

Example: You trade one standard lot of EUR/USD. Spread cost: 0.2 pips = $2. Commission: $6. Total cost: $8.

Which is cheaper?

It depends on three things:

  • How often you trade. If you open two trades a month, a couple of extra pips won't hurt. If you scalp ten times a day, every fractional pip compounds.
  • How many pips you're targeting. A 50-pip swing trade can absorb a 1.5-pip spread. A 5-pip scalp cannot.
  • Your position size. Commissions are fixed per lot. Spreads scale with size, but the percentage cost changes depending on how long you hold.

### A quick comparison (EUR/USD, 1 standard lot)

| Account type | Spread | Commission | Total cost | |--------------|--------|------------|------------| | Standard | 1.5 pips | $0 | $15 | | ECN | 0.2 pips | $6 | $8 |

For a scalper trying to grab 5–8 pips, that $7 difference per trade is the difference between profit and loss.

The Philippine context

Many brokers serving Filipinos offer both account types. When you're comparing, convert commission to pesos at current rates and compare against the pip cost in your typical trade size.

If you're funding with GCash or a local bank transfer and your broker charges in USD, factor in the conversion spread too — that's another hidden cost.

The psychological difference

Standard accounts feel cheaper because there's no line item. ECN accounts make the cost explicit. Humans hate seeing fees. But explicit is better. You can measure it, track it, and optimize around it.

Next: Day 17 — What is a pip, exactly?

posts.title: How bid, ask, and spread work together
posts.titleText: How bid, ask, and spread work together
posts.lede: You see EUR/USD quoted 1.0850 / 1.0852. The left is the bid. The right is the ask. The 2-pip gap is the spread. If you buy, you enter at 1.0852. To break even, the bid must rise to 1.0852. You start u
posts.heroAlt: Day 017 of 404 — How bid, ask, and spread work together
posts.body:
The quote you see

Open any forex platform and you'll see a two-sided price. Let's use EUR/USD as the example:

1.0850 / 1.0852

The left number is the bid — the price at which the market will buy euros from you (or, if you're short, the price you pay to close).

The right number is the ask — the price at which the market will sell euros to you (or, if you're long, the price you pay to open).

The gap between them — in this case 2 pips — is the spread. It's the broker's cut, the market's transaction cost, and your first obstacle.

What happens when you buy

You believe the euro will strengthen. You click buy. Your platform executes at the ask: 1.0852.

Now look at your open position. Most platforms will show an unrealised profit/loss immediately. What does it say?

–2 pips.

You haven't held the trade for even one second. The price hasn't moved. But you're already down.

Why you start negative

Because if you closed that position right now, you'd exit at the bid: 1.0850. You bought at 1.0852. The difference is the spread, and you paid it the instant you entered.

This is not a bug. It's not your broker cheating you. It's the structure of the market. The spread is the cost of doing business, and it's deducted up front as an unrealised loss.

What it takes to break even

For your trade to show zero profit or loss, the bid must rise to match your entry price.

You entered at 1.0852 (the ask). Break-even happens when the bid reaches 1.0852. At that point, the quote might look like 1.0852 / 1.0854 — the market has moved 2 pips in your favor, and you've clawed back the spread.

Only after that do you start making money.

A Filipino scenario

Imagine you're a Makati-based trader. You open a 0.10-lot EUR/USD long at 1.0852. Your position size means each pip is worth about ₱50.

The moment you enter, you're down ₱100. The price hasn't moved. You just paid the spread.

If EUR/USD rallies to 1.0860 (8 pips), your unrealised profit is not ₱400. It's ₱300 — because the first 2 pips went to covering the spread.

Why this matters

Most beginners don't realize the spread is a cost per trade, not a one-time account fee. If you open and close ten trades in a day, you pay the spread ten times. Scalpers and high-frequency traders live or die by spread size.

It also means that tight spreads matter more the shorter your holding period. If you're swing trading over days or weeks, a 2-pip spread is noise. If you're trying to scalp 5-pip moves, that same spread just ate 40% of your target.

The honest truth

You are not starting from zero when you enter a trade. You are starting from negative. The market does not owe you a win just because you clicked a button. Your first job is to recover what you paid to get in.

Next: Day 18 — What is a pip, exactly?

posts.title: What is the order book? (And why you can't see it)
posts.titleText: What is the order book? (And why you can't see it)
posts.lede: In stock trading, the order book is public: you see every buy and sell order waiting at each price. In forex, there is no central order book. The market is over-the-counter, decentralized. Some broker
posts.heroAlt: Day 018 of 404 — What is the order book? (And why you can't see it)
posts.body:
If you've ever traded stocks on the Philippine Stock Exchange or watched a US equity platform, you've probably seen the order book — a live list of all the buy orders (bids) and sell orders (asks) waiting at each price level. It's public. Everyone sees the same thing.

Forex is different.

Forex has no central order book

Forex is an over-the-counter (OTC) market. That means there's no single exchange where all orders are routed and displayed. Instead, trading happens through a decentralized network of banks, brokers, hedge funds, and market makers — all quoting prices to each other, often through private relationships.

There is no "master list" of pending orders. No ticker tape. No unified depth chart that everyone can see.

What your broker shows you

Some brokers — especially those offering ECN (Electronic Communication Network) accounts — do provide what's called Level II data or market depth. This is a window into the orders sitting on their liquidity providers' books.

You might see something like this:

  • 56.52 — 2.5 million USD to sell
  • 56.50 — 4.0 million USD to buy
  • 56.48 — 1.8 million USD to buy

That's useful. But it's not the whole market. It's a slice — one broker's view of one network's liquidity at one moment.

Why it matters for scalpers

If you're trying to scalp 5–15 pips on a pair like USD/PHP, knowing where clusters of buy or sell orders sit can help you anticipate where price might stall, bounce, or break through.

Let's say you see a thick wall of buy orders at 56.50. That suggests institutional players or algo systems are willing to defend that level. Price may pause there. If it breaks, those orders get filled and the next support level comes into play.

It's not a guarantee. It's a hint — and in a market with no public order book, hints matter.

A Manila example

Imagine you're a trader in Makati watching USD/PHP during the 4 p.m. BSP fix window. Your broker's Level II shows a large sell order at 56.55. That might be a corporate client converting dollar receivables into pesos for payroll. If that order absorbs all the buy-side momentum, price stalls. If buyers push through it, you get a breakout.

You didn't know it would happen. But you saw the setup.

The limitation

Remember: what you see is not exhaustive. A big bank in Singapore might have a huge order sitting elsewhere that never shows up on your screen. Price can slice through your broker's "support" like it wasn't there — because globally, it wasn't.

Treat Level II as context, not prophecy.

Next: Day 19 — What is market depth?

posts.title: Why volume in forex isn't what you think
posts.titleText: Why volume in forex isn't what you think
posts.lede: Forex has no central exchange, so there's no official volume count. What your broker shows is tick volume — the number of price changes, not the number of contracts traded. It's a proxy for activity,
posts.heroAlt: Day 019 of 404 — Why volume in forex isn't what you think
posts.body:
The problem with volume in forex

If you've traded stocks before — or even just watched stock charts — you know the volume bar at the bottom of the screen. It tells you how many shares changed hands in a given period. High volume during a breakout? That's confirmation. Low volume on a rally? Suspect.

In forex, that same bar exists. But it doesn't mean the same thing.

Why forex volume is different

Forex is decentralised. There is no single exchange that records every transaction. The market is a network of banks, brokers, hedge funds, and retail platforms. Each one sees only its own flow.

Your broker has no idea what happened at another broker. The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas has no obligation to report its interventions in real time. A Singapore bank trading with a Tokyo counterparty never publishes that data.

So when your MetaTrader chart shows a volume bar, what is it actually showing?

Tick volume: the proxy

Most retail platforms display tick volume — the number of times the price changed during a given period. Not the number of lots traded. Not the dollar value exchanged. Just the count of price updates.

If EUR/USD ticked 400 times in one minute, your volume bar shows 400. If it ticked 50 times the next minute, the bar shrinks.

Tick volume is a proxy for activity. When real participation is high, price moves more often. When the market is quiet, ticks slow down.

When tick volume is useful

You can use tick volume relatively:

  • A breakout with high tick volume is more credible than one with low ticks.
  • A spike in tick volume during London open tells you participants showed up.
  • Comparing this hour's ticks to the prior hour can reveal a shift in intensity.

But you cannot use it absolutely. You can't say "this move had strong volume, so it's confirmed" the way you might in stocks.

The trap: stock indicators ported to forex

Many classic indicators — On-Balance Volume, Chaikin Money Flow, Volume-Weighted Average Price — were designed for markets with real volume data. Applying them to forex tick volume is like using a thermometer to measure distance. The math still runs. The result is nonsense.

A Filipino example

Imagine you're watching USD/PHP during a BSP rate decision. Your broker's volume bar spikes. Does that mean the central bank intervened? Maybe. Or maybe your broker's liquidity provider saw a surge in retail orders. Or maybe the feed lagged and caught up all at once.

You don't know. You can't know. The spike tells you something happened, but not what or how much.

The takeaway

Forex volume is a shadow. It hints at activity but never proves it. Use it for context — to compare one period to another, to spot unusual participation — but never treat it as ground truth.

If an indicator relies heavily on volume, ask whether it was built for centralised markets. If yes, be skeptical.

Next: Day 20 — What is a pip?

posts.title: What is a lot in forex?
posts.titleText: What is a lot in forex?
posts.lede: A lot is the unit that measures trade size. A standard lot is 100,000 units of the base currency. A mini lot is 10,000. A micro lot is 1,000. A nano lot is 100. Why it matters: lot size determines how
posts.heroAlt: Day 020 of 404 — What is a lot in forex?
posts.body:
The unit no one explains clearly

When someone says they "bought EUR/USD," the next question should be: how much? In forex, that answer is always given in lots — the standardized unit of trade size.

A lot isn't slang. It's not approximate. It's a contract-size definition that every broker, platform, and trader uses to measure position size.

The four lot sizes

Here's the breakdown:

  • Standard lot: 100,000 units of the base currency
  • Mini lot: 10,000 units
  • Micro lot: 1,000 units
  • Nano lot: 100 units

If you open 1 standard lot of EUR/USD, you're controlling €100,000 worth of exposure. If you open 1 micro lot, you're controlling €1,000.

Most retail traders in the Philippines start with micro or nano lots. That's not a limitation — it's risk management.

Why lot size is the first real decision you make

Lot size is what turns abstract price movement into actual money. Let's say EUR/USD moves 10 pips in your favor.

  • On a nano lot (100 units), that's roughly ₱5.
  • On a micro lot (1,000 units), that's roughly ₱50.
  • On a mini lot (10,000 units), that's roughly ₱500.
  • On a standard lot (100,000 units), that's roughly ₱5,000.

Same chart. Same direction. Same 10 pips. The only variable is the size you chose.

A real scenario: OFW remittance hedging

Imagine a kababayan working in Dubai expects to send home $2,000 next month. Right now USD/PHP is at 56.50, so that's ₱113,000. But if the peso strengthens to 55.00 by next month, the same $2,000 becomes ₱110,000 — a ₱3,000 loss in purchasing power.

If this person wanted to hedge that exposure using forex, they'd need to think in lot sizes. A micro lot of USD/PHP (1,000 units) represents $1,000 of exposure. To hedge $2,000, they'd use 2 micro lots — or 0.02 standard lots.

This is not a recommendation to hedge remittances via retail forex. It's an illustration: lot size is the bridge between abstract currency units and real-world money.

Lot size is leverage's twin

You'll hear a lot about leverage soon (we'll cover it properly in a future post). But here's the preview: leverage allows you to control a large lot with a small deposit. A standard lot might require only $1,000 in margin at 100:1 leverage.

That sounds like a gift. It's actually a test. If you don't understand lot size, leverage becomes a way to lose money faster than you thought possible.

What to remember

Lot size is not complicated. It's just a unit. But it's the unit that matters most when a trade goes live, because it's the multiplier on every pip of movement — in both directions.

Next: Day 21 — What is the base currency and quote currency?

posts.title: What lot sizes actually mean
posts.titleText: What lot sizes actually mean
posts.lede: A lot is how much currency you control. On EUR/USD, 1 standard lot = $10 per pip. 1 mini lot = $1/pip. 1 micro lot = $0.10/pip. Filipino math: a 30-pip stop-loss on a micro lot = $3, or roughly ₱170.
posts.heroAlt: Day 021 of 404 — What lot sizes actually mean
posts.body:
You've learned what a pip is. Now we need to talk about what a pip costs — because that number changes depending on how much currency you're controlling. That "how much" is called your lot size.

The three standard lot sizes

Forex brokers offer three main position sizes:

  • Standard lot: 100,000 units of the base currency
  • Mini lot: 10,000 units
  • Micro lot: 1,000 units

On EUR/USD, the math is clean:

  • 1 standard lot = $10 per pip
  • 1 mini lot = $1 per pip
  • 1 micro lot = $0.10 per pip

If EUR/USD moves 30 pips against you and you're trading one standard lot, you just lost $300. If you're on a micro lot, that same move costs you $3.

Filipino math: what does this actually mean?

Let's say you're testing a breakout strategy. You set a 30-pip stop-loss — tight, but reasonable for intraday price action.

  • On a standard lot: 30 pips × $10 = $300 ≈ ₱17,000
  • On a mini lot: 30 pips × $1 = $30 ≈ ₱1,700
  • On a micro lot: 30 pips × $0.10 = $3 ≈ ₱170

Most Filipinos starting out don't have ₱17,000 to risk on a single idea. But ₱170? That's the cost of learning without the fear.

Why beginners should start on micro lots

Trading is a skill. Skills take repetition. Repetition requires surviving your mistakes long enough to stop making them.

If you start on standard lots with a ₱50,000 account, five bad trades can cut you in half. Emotionally, that's hard to recover from. You start revenge-trading. You chase. You stop following your plan.

Start on micro lots. Take 50 trades. Watch what happens when you move your stop too close, when you enter too early, when you ignore your checklist. The financial damage will be small. The educational value will not.

A note on other pairs

Pip value changes slightly depending on the currency pair and your account currency. On USD/JPY, GBP/USD, or crosses like EUR/GBP, the math is different. Most brokers show pip value in real time on the trade ticket. Check it before you click.

The real question

Lot size is not about ego. It's about how long you stay in the game.

If you're still learning to read price action, manage emotion, and follow a plan, there is zero reason to trade anything larger than a micro lot. Zero.

Next: Day 22 — What is margin?

posts.title: What is leverage, really?
posts.titleText: What is leverage, really?
posts.lede: Leverage is borrowed capital from your broker. A 1:100 ratio means your $100 controls a $10,000 position. Brokers offer it because forex moves are tiny — a 1% daily swing is huge. But here's the part
posts.heroAlt: Day 022 of 404 — What is leverage, really?
posts.body:
The definition

Leverage is borrowed capital provided by your broker that allows you to control a position larger than the cash you have in your account.

If your broker offers 1:100 leverage, that means every ₱1 you deposit can control ₱100 worth of currency. Put in ₱5,000, and you can open a position worth ₱500,000.

That's not magic. It's a loan. And like any loan, it has consequences.

Why brokers offer it

Forex price moves are small. A 1% move in a single day is considered large. Most pairs move 0.3–0.8% on a normal session.

If you traded ₱10,000 of your own money with no leverage and the pair moved 0.5% in your favor, you'd make ₱50. That's not enough to cover the spread on most trades, let alone make trading worth your time.

Leverage exists to make small percentage moves feel meaningful. It lets retail traders participate in a market originally built for institutions moving millions.

The math everyone skips

Let's say you open a USD/PHP position worth ₱100,000 using 1:100 leverage. You only need ₱1,000 in your account as margin.

  • If the pair moves 1% in your favor, you make ₱1,000. You just doubled your money.
  • If it moves 1% against you, you lose ₱1,000. Your account is now zero.

Notice the symmetry. Leverage doesn't care which way the market goes. It amplifies both.

A local example

Imagine you're a Makati-based trader with ₱10,000 in your account. You use 1:50 leverage to open a ₱500,000 EUR/USD position.

EUR/USD drops 0.5%. That's a tiny move — barely noticed by institutions. But for you, that's a ₱2,500 loss. Your ₱10,000 account is now ₱7,500.

One more 0.5% move and you're at ₱5,000. Three bad trades in a week, and you're done — not because you're a bad analyst, but because the position size was too large for the capital you had.

Why it's misunderstood

Beginners see leverage as a way to "make more money faster." That's backward.

Leverage is a position-sizing tool. It determines how much market movement your account can survive. Used correctly, it lets you stay small and controlled. Used incorrectly, it turns every trade into a coin flip with your rent money.

The hard truth

Most retail traders don't blow up because they picked the wrong direction. They blow up because they used too much leverage on a trade that was right in theory but hit their stop-loss before the market turned.

The market doesn't care how confident you are. Leverage makes confidence expensive.

What to remember

  • Leverage is not optional in forex — even "no leverage" accounts use some, because of how lot sizes work.
  • Higher leverage is not a feature. It's a responsibility.
  • Your broker will let you use 1:500. That doesn't mean you should.
  • Position size matters more than leverage ratio. A small position at 1:100 is safer than a large position at 1:10.

Next: Day 23 — What is margin?

posts.title: What is margin in forex?
posts.titleText: What is margin in forex?
posts.lede: Margin is the deposit your broker holds while a trade is open. It's not a fee — it's collateral. With 1:100 leverage, a $10,000 position requires $100 margin. When you close the trade, that $100 is re
posts.heroAlt: Day 023 of 404 — What is margin in forex?
posts.body:
The confusion around margin

Ask a new trader what margin is, and you'll hear guesses: "It's a fee," "It's what you lose when the trade goes bad," "It's the broker's cut." None of those are right.

Margin is simpler than it sounds. It's the collateral your broker holds while a leveraged trade is open. Think of it as a security deposit — like what you pay when you rent an apartment. When you move out (close the trade), you get it back.

How margin works in practice

Let's say you want to open a position worth $10,000 in EUR/USD. Your broker offers 1:100 leverage. That means you only need to put up 1% of the position size as margin.

1% of $10,000 = $100 margin required.

Your broker locks that $100 from your account balance. It's still yours — it's just reserved. You can't use it to open another trade until this one closes.

When you close the position, win or lose, that $100 is released back into your available balance.

Margin is not a fee

This is the key insight. The broker does not take your margin. It doesn't disappear. It's temporarily set aside.

What you actually lose (or gain) is determined by how the market moves and where you close the trade. That profit or loss is separate from margin.

A Filipino example

Imagine you're a freelancer who uses GCash. A client asks you to hold ₱5,000 in your wallet as a "good faith deposit" while a project is ongoing. You still own that ₱5,000 — you just can't spend it until the project ends. When it's done, the hold is lifted.

Margin works the same way. Your broker holds a slice of your balance while the trade is live, then releases it when you're out.

Why brokers require margin

Leverage lets you control a large position with a small account. But leverage also means risk. If the trade moves against you, the broker needs assurance that you can cover potential losses.

Margin is that assurance. It's the broker's way of saying, "You can borrow our capital to amplify your trade, but we're holding collateral in case things go wrong."

What happens if margin runs low

If your trade moves against you and your account equity drops, your free margin (the amount available for new trades) shrinks. If it drops too far, you hit a margin call — a warning that you're close to not having enough collateral to keep your positions open.

We'll cover margin calls in detail later. For now, just understand: margin is what you reserve. Equity is what you have left after accounting for open profit or loss.

The takeaway

Margin is not mysterious. It's not a hidden cost. It's a deposit that gets returned when the trade closes.

Most retail traders lose money not because they don't understand margin, but because they open positions so large that a small move wipes out their equity. Margin is the mechanic. Position sizing is the decision that matters.

Next: Day 24 — What is free margin?

posts.title: What margin call and stop out actually mean
posts.titleText: What margin call and stop out actually mean
posts.lede: A margin call is your broker's warning that your account equity is dangerously low — close to the margin required to keep positions open. A stop out is what happens next: the broker closes your trades
posts.heroAlt: Day 024 of 404 — What margin call and stop out actually mean
posts.body:
What a margin call is

A margin call happens when your account equity drops close to the margin required to keep your open positions alive. It's a warning — not a liquidation, not yet. Your broker is telling you: "Add more money, or close some trades, or we'll do it for you."

Different brokers set different thresholds. Some will notify you at 100% margin level (equity equals used margin). Others wait until 80%. The number varies, but the message is the same: you're running out of room.

What stop out means

If you don't act — or if the market moves too fast for you to react — the broker will trigger a stop out. This is an automatic closure of your positions, usually when your margin level falls to 50% or lower.

The broker isn't punishing you. It's protecting itself. Leverage means you're trading with borrowed money. If your equity falls below what you owe, the broker is on the hook. Stop out is the circuit breaker that prevents that.

A Filipino example

Let's say you deposit ₱10,000 into a broker account. You open a 0.5-lot position on USD/PHP at 1:100 leverage. The required margin is around ₱2,800. Your equity is ₱10,000, so your margin level is roughly 357%.

Now the trade moves against you. You're down ₱7,500. Your equity is now ₱2,500. Your margin level has dropped to about 89%. You get a margin call warning.

You ignore it. Price keeps moving. Your equity hits ₱1,400. Margin level: 50%. The broker closes your position automatically. You're left with ₱1,400 in your account — a realized loss of ₱8,600.

You didn't "lose to the broker." You lost to position size and leverage you couldn't handle.

The hard truth

If you've ever been margin-called or stopped out, the mistake wasn't in that moment. It was three decisions earlier:

  • You opened a position too large for your account.
  • You didn't set a stop loss, or set it too wide.
  • You added to a losing trade instead of cutting it.

Margin call is the symptom. Overleveraging is the disease.

What to do instead

  • Never use more than 1–2% of your account equity as risk per trade.
  • Always know your margin level before you open a position.
  • Set a stop loss that gets you out long before your broker has to.

If your broker ever has to close a trade for you, you've already failed the test.

Next: Day 25 — What is a pip?

posts.title: Reading your broker's status line: Equity, Balance, Free Margin
posts.titleText: Reading your broker's status line: Equity, Balance, Free Margin
posts.lede: Your broker shows three numbers at the top of every platform. Balance is your deposit plus or minus closed trades. Equity is balance plus any open profit or loss right now. Free margin is equity minus
posts.heroAlt: Day 025 of 404 — Reading your broker's status line: Equity, Balance, Free Margin
posts.body:
The three numbers every platform shows you

Open any retail forex platform — MT4, MT5, cTrader, your broker's web terminal — and somewhere near the top you'll see a status line that looks like this:

  • Balance: ₱50,000
  • Equity: ₱48,200
  • Free Margin: ₱46,500

Most beginners glance at balance, assume that's their account size, and move on. That's a mistake. Each of these three numbers tells you something different, and confusing them is one of the fastest ways to blow past your risk limits without realizing it.

Balance: your closed history

Balance is your starting deposit, plus or minus every trade you've closed. It does not move while a position is open. If you deposited ₱50,000 and you're currently holding a trade that's down ₱1,800, your balance still shows ₱50,000.

Balance only updates the moment you close.

Think of it as your account's "official" ledger — but it's always slightly out of date if you have anything open.

Equity: the live truth

Equity is balance plus (or minus) the floating profit or loss of every open position, calculated in real time.

If your balance is ₱50,000 and you have one open trade losing ₱1,800, your equity is ₱48,200. If that trade swings into profit by ₱500, equity becomes ₱50,500. Balance hasn't moved. Equity tracks reality.

This is the number that matters for margin calls. Your broker doesn't care what your balance was yesterday. It cares what your equity is right now.

Free margin: permission to trade

Free margin is equity minus the margin you've already committed to open positions.

Let's say your equity is ₱48,200 and you have ₱1,700 tied up as margin in an open trade. Your free margin is ₱46,500. That ₱46,500 is what you can still use to open new trades.

When free margin hits zero, your platform will reject any new order. When equity falls below your broker's margin call threshold (often 100% or 50% of used margin), positions start getting closed automatically.

A concrete example: three trades, one account

You deposit ₱50,000.

  • You open Trade A. It requires ₱2,000 margin. Balance: ₱50,000. Equity: ₱50,000. Free margin: ₱48,000.
  • Trade A moves against you by ₱1,500. Balance: still ₱50,000. Equity: ₱48,500. Free margin: ₱46,500.
  • You open Trade B. It needs ₱1,800 margin. Balance: ₱50,000. Equity: ₱48,500. Free margin: ₱44,700.
  • Trade B gains ₱800. Trade A is still losing ₱1,500. Balance: ₱50,000. Equity: ₱49,300. Free margin: ₱45,500.

Notice: balance never moved. Equity and free margin moved every tick.

Why beginners get this wrong

Because balance looks stable, it feels safe. It's the number that matches your deposit receipt. But if you're managing risk by watching balance, you're flying blind.

Equity is your actual account value. Free margin is your remaining room to maneuver. Both matter more than balance the moment you have an open trade.

The takeaway

Before you open your next position, make it a habit: glance at equity, check free margin, confirm you have room. This is not paranoia. It's cockpit discipline.

The status line is boring until the one day it isn't.

Next: Day 26 — What is a margin call, and why does it happen?

posts.title: What is drawdown, and why it hurts
posts.titleText: What is drawdown, and why it hurts
posts.lede: Drawdown is the percentage your account has fallen from its highest point. If you peak at ₱50,000 and drop to ₱35,000, that's a 30% drawdown. The pain: you now need a +43% gain just to break even. Thi
posts.heroAlt: Day 026 of 404 — What is drawdown, and why it hurts
posts.body:
What drawdown actually measures

Drawdown is the percentage decline from the highest point (peak) your account has reached to the lowest point (trough) before it recovers. It's measured on your equity curve — the line that tracks your account balance over time.

If your account grows from ₱30,000 to ₱50,000, then falls to ₱35,000, your drawdown is:

(50,000 − 35,000) ÷ 50,000 = 30%

You're now 30% below your peak.

The cruel asymmetry

Here's the part that surprises new traders: losses and gains are not symmetrical.

If you lose 30%, you need to gain 43% to get back to breakeven. Lose 50%, and you need to double your remaining capital — a 100% return — just to recover.

The math:

  • Start: ₱50,000
  • Lose 30%: ₱35,000 remains
  • To recover: ₱35,000 × 1.43 = ₱50,050

That 43% climb is steeper, slower, and psychologically harder than the 30% fall.

Why professionals obsess over max drawdown

Every strategy — whether it's a trading system, a fund, or your own manual approach — has a maximum historical drawdown: the worst peak-to-trough loss it has ever experienced.

A strategy that averages 50% annual returns sounds great. But if its max drawdown is 60%, most retail traders won't survive it. They'll panic, stop following the rules, or quit entirely during the trough.

Drawdown is the filter that separates theoretical performance from tradable reality.

A local example

Imagine a Makati-based trader starts with ₱100,000. After six good months, the account grows to ₱150,000. Then a rough stretch hits: poor trade timing, a surprise BSP rate hold, and one overleveraged position. The account falls to ₱105,000.

Drawdown: (150,000 − 105,000) ÷ 150,000 = 30%

To get back to ₱150,000, the trader now needs: (150,000 − 105,000) ÷ 105,000 ≈ 43%

That's not six months of work. That could be a year — or more — depending on consistency and market conditions.

Why risk limits exist

This is why experienced traders set hard rules:

  • Maximum loss per trade: 1–2% of account equity
  • Maximum daily loss: 5%
  • Maximum drawdown before taking a break: 10–15%

These aren't arbitrary. They're designed to keep drawdown small enough that recovery is mathematically realistic and psychologically bearable.

Profit is exciting. But drawdown is what kills accounts.

Next: Day 27 — What is equity vs. balance?

posts.title: What is Profit Factor?
posts.titleText: What is Profit Factor?
posts.lede: Profit factor is gross profit divided by gross loss. A result above 1.0 means your strategy made money. Above 1.5 is solid. Beginners chase high win rates — 70%, 80% — but profit factor tells the real
posts.heroAlt: Day 027 of 404 — What is Profit Factor?
posts.body:
The formula

Profit Factor = Gross Profit ÷ Gross Loss

That's it. Add up everything you made on winning trades. Add up everything you lost on losing trades. Divide the first number by the second.

  • If the result is greater than 1.0, your strategy made money.
  • If it's less than 1.0, you lost money.
  • If it's above 1.5, you have a solid edge.

Why beginners get this wrong

New traders love to talk about win rate. "I'm right 75% of the time!" sounds impressive. And it feels good — being right usually does.

But here's the problem: win rate doesn't tell you how much you made when you won or how much you gave back when you lost.

Consider two traders over 10 trades:

Trader A: Wins 7 out of 10. Each win = ₱500. Each loss = ₱2,000. Total profit = ₱3,500. Total loss = ₱6,000. Profit factor = 3,500 ÷ 6,000 = 0.58 Result: Lost money.

Trader B: Wins 4 out of 10. Each win = ₱3,000. Each loss = ₱800. Total profit = ₱12,000. Total loss = ₱4,800. Profit factor = 12,000 ÷ 4,800 = 2.5 Result: Made money.

Trader B was "wrong" more often. Trader B made more money. That's profit factor at work.

A Filipino example

Imagine you're testing a breakout strategy on USD/PHP. Over one month:

  • 12 winning trades, total gain: ₱18,000
  • 8 losing trades, total loss: ₱10,000

Profit factor = 18,000 ÷ 10,000 = 1.8

That's a strong result. It means for every peso you risk and lose, you're making ₱1.80 back on average. The strategy has an edge — assuming you can keep executing it the same way.

What's a "good" profit factor?

  • 1.0–1.25: Barely profitable. Vulnerable to slippage, spread, and mistakes.
  • 1.25–1.5: Workable, but needs discipline.
  • 1.5–2.0: Solid edge.
  • Above 2.0: Rare in real trading. If you see this in a backtest, be skeptical — it probably won't survive live market conditions.

Why it matters more than win rate

Profit factor forces you to think about risk management and reward-to-risk ratio. It doesn't let you hide behind "I'm usually right." It asks the harder question: Are you profitable?

Most retail traders lose money not because they can't pick direction, but because they risk too much on each trade and let losses run. Profit factor exposes that immediately.

Next: Day 28 — What is a pip?

posts.title: Why keep a trading journal?
posts.titleText: Why keep a trading journal?
posts.lede: A trading journal is not a diary. It's a performance tool. Log every trade: date, pair, direction, entry, stop, target, result, reason, and a screenshot. Review weekly. Without it, you can't learn fro
posts.heroAlt: Day 028 of 404 — Why keep a trading journal?
posts.body:
A journal is not a diary

A trading journal is not where you write how you feel about the market. It's where you log what you did, why you did it, and what happened. It's a performance tool — the same kind an athlete or a surgeon would use to get better at a repeatable skill.

Most traders skip this step. Most traders lose money. The two facts are related.

What to log (minimum)

Every trade should have a record that includes:

  • Date and time (including your timezone — useful if you trade London vs. New York hours)
  • Pair (e.g., USD/PHP, EUR/USD)
  • Direction (long or short)
  • Entry price
  • Stop-loss level
  • Target level (if you had one)
  • Exit price (actual)
  • Result (pips gained/lost, peso P&L)
  • Reason for entry (one sentence: "Broke above 56.50 resistance, bullish RSI divergence")
  • Screenshot of the chart at entry

If you use a notes app, a Google Sheet, or a dedicated journal like Edgewonk or Notion, it doesn't matter. What matters is that it's consistent and you actually use it.

Why it works

A journal does three things:

1. It forces you to have a reason. If you can't write down why you took a trade, you probably shouldn't have taken it. 2. It creates reviewable data. After 20 trades, patterns emerge. You'll see that your best trades came during the London session, or that you lose money every time you chase a breakout without confirmation. 3. It separates luck from skill. One winning trade means nothing. Ten trades with the same setup and a 70% win rate — that's signal.

A local example

Imagine you're a part-time trader in Manila. You work 9–6, so you trade the New York close. Over two months, you log 30 trades. When you review, you notice:

  • You win 65% of the time on USD/PHP when you enter after the BSP rate decision.
  • You lose 80% of the time when you trade during your lunch break, distracted, no clear setup.

That's not theory. That's your data. Now you have something actionable.

The hard truth

Most blown accounts never kept a journal. They repeated the same mistakes because they never measured them. You can't fix what you don't track.

If you're serious about improving, the journal isn't optional. It's the difference between trading and guessing.

Next: Day 29 — What is a pip?

posts.title: Why demo trading can't teach you to trade
posts.titleText: Why demo trading can't teach you to trade
posts.lede: Demo accounts are for learning buttons and order types. They are not for learning trading. When it's fake money, fear disappears — and fear is half the job. Your first live trade, even ₱100, will teac
posts.heroAlt: Day 029 of 404 — Why demo trading can't teach you to trade
posts.body:
The illusion of competence

Demo accounts are useful. They let you learn where the "buy" button is, how to set a stop-loss, what happens when you fat-finger a lot size. But they create a dangerous illusion: that you're learning to trade.

You're not. You're learning to use software.

What demo can't simulate

The difference between demo and live isn't technical. It's emotional.

When you place a trade with fake money:

  • You don't feel fear when the price moves against you.
  • You don't feel greed when it moves in your favor.
  • You don't feel regret when you close early and it keeps running.
  • You don't refresh your account balance obsessively.
  • You don't lie awake replaying a loss.

All of that shows up the moment real money is on the line — even if it's just ₱100.

The emotional gap is where traders break

You can be profitable on demo for six months straight and still blow your first live account in two weeks. It happens all the time. The strategy didn't fail. The person did — because they'd never trained the part of themselves that demo can't reach.

A concrete example

Imagine you're a Manila-based trader. On demo, you risk $10 per trade (fake dollars). You lose three in a row. You shrug and open the fourth.

Now imagine the same scenario live, but you're risking ₱500 per trade — half a day's budget for groceries. You lose three in a row. That's ₱1,500. Your hand hovers over the fourth trade. You hesitate. You skip it. It wins. Now you're angry.

That sequence — hesitation, skip, regret, anger — never happens on demo. But it's the real curriculum.

The right way to use demo

Demo is for mechanics. Use it to answer questions like:

  • How do I set a stop-loss?
  • What happens if I close half a position?
  • How does my broker calculate margin?
  • Can I trail a stop manually, or does the platform do it?

Two to four weeks is enough for that. Once you know where the buttons are and you've placed 20–30 practice trades to build muscle memory, stop.

Go live at the smallest size possible

Most Philippine brokers let you trade micro lots — positions worth ₱50 to ₱200 of risk per trade. Start there.

It won't feel like much. That's the point. You're not trying to make money yet. You're trying to learn how you behave when the outcome matters.

Do you follow your plan, or do you improvise? Do you close early out of fear? Do you revenge-trade after a loss?

You will never learn the answers on demo.

The hard truth

Most retail traders lose money. The majority of that loss comes not from bad strategy, but from emotional mistakes: overtrading, revenge trading, moving stops, cutting winners early, letting losers run.

Demo doesn't prepare you for any of that. Your first live account does.

Treat it like tuition. Keep the position size small enough that a loss stings but doesn't hurt. That's the zone where learning happens.

posts.titleText: Month 1 complete: 29 concepts down
posts.lede: You've made it through the first month. Twenty-nine terms. Pairs, pips, spreads, leverage, margin, sessions, liquidity, order types, central banks. This was the vocabulary layer. Without it, nothing e
posts.heroAlt: Day 030 of 404 — Month 1 complete: 29 concepts down
posts.body:
You made it through Month 1.

Twenty-nine weekdays. Twenty-nine concepts. If you've been reading since Day 1, you now have a working vocabulary for forex. You know what a currency pair is, how pips and lots work, what leverage does, why the spread exists, when liquidity peaks, and how central banks move markets.

That might not sound like much. But it's everything.

### What Month 1 was for

Most people who lose money in forex do so because they skip this part. They open a demo account, place a trade, watch the number go up or down, and assume they understand what's happening. They don't.

Month 1 was the cost of entry. The vocabulary layer. You can't read price action if you don't know what a pip is. You can't manage risk if you don't understand margin. You can't interpret news if you've never heard of a dovish central bank statement.

We built the foundation slowly, one term at a time, because that's the only way it sticks.

### A quick recap of what we covered

Here's the map:

  • What forex is and why it exists (Days 1–2)
  • Currency pairs: base, quote, majors, minors, exotics (Days 3–6)
  • Pips, pipettes, and lot sizes — the units of movement and position size (Days 7–10)
  • Leverage and margin — the double-edged tools that define retail forex (Days 11–14)
  • Bid, ask, and spread — the built-in cost of every trade (Days 15–17)
  • Market sessions and when liquidity actually matters (Days 18–21)
  • Order types: market, limit, stop, stop-loss, take-profit (Days 22–26)
  • Central banks and interest rates — the biggest single driver of currency prices (Days 27–29)

Twenty-nine ideas. None of them optional.

### What changes in Month 2

Starting tomorrow, we pivot from vocabulary to observation. You'll learn to read a chart. What a candlestick is. What support and resistance mean. How to spot a trend and when it's actually just noise.

This is where it gets harder.

Definitions are clean. Charts are messy. Price doesn't move in straight lines. Patterns fail. Support breaks. Trends reverse without warning. And unlike vocabulary, there's no single right answer—just better and worse ways to interpret what you're seeing.

Month 2 will feel slower. That's by design.

### A note for Filipino readers

If you're an OFW, a BPO worker in Metro Manila, or someone in the provinces watching YouTube forex videos at night after your day job—this series is for you. Not because forex is your ticket out. It's not. Most retail traders lose money, and that will stay true no matter how many posts you read.

But if you're going to try, you deserve to start with the truth. No hype. No shortcuts. Just the actual map.

You've done one month. That puts you ahead of everyone who quit on Day 3 because it wasn't flashy enough.

### What to do next

If you missed any posts, go back. The order matters. Day 12 won't make sense if you skipped Day 8.

If you've been taking notes—good. Keep doing that. Write down the terms in your own words. Test yourself. Use them in sentences. Make them yours.

And if you've been itching to open a chart and "just try it," hold off one more month. Let the foundation set. Month 2 will get you there.

The vocabulary is done. The real work begins now.
